claim: VIP-expressing interneurons represent 15-20% of cortical interneurons and are located mostly in the upper layers of the cortex.
source: Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) expression demarcates a small interneuron subpopulation (15–20%) located mostly in the upper layers of the cortex (Kim et al., 2017; Staiger et al., 2004; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 1997; Gonchar et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Kim et al., 2017; Staiger et al., 2004; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 1997; Gonchar et al., 2007).

claim: VIP interneurons preferentially inhibit other interneurons and thereby disinhibit principal neurons.
source: Previous studies have identified a cortical circuit motif controlled by VIP interneurons that preferentially inhibit other interneurons and thereby disinhibit principal neurons (Lee et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).

claim: VIP interneurons mainly inhibit somatostatin interneurons, which exert inhibitory drive on the dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In this circuit, VIP interneurons mainly inhibit somatostatin interneurons, which tend to exert an inhibitory drive on the dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons (Gentet et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gentet et al., 2012.

claim: The same stereotyped VIP connectivity was found in functionally and cytoarchitectonically different regions including auditory, prefrontal, visual, somatosensory cortices, amygdala, and hippocampus.
source: The same stereotyped connectivity was found in functionally and cytoarchitectonically different regions of the brain, across the auditory, prefrontal (Pi et al., 2013), visual (Pfeffer et al., 2013), and somatosensory (SS; Gasselin et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013) cortices, as well as in the amygdala (Krabbe et al., 2019) and the hippocampus (Francavilla et al., 2018; Tyan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in different brain regions (Pi et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Gasselin et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013; Krabbe et al., 2019; Francavilla et al., 2018; Tyan et al., 2014).

claim: VIP interneurons in auditory cortex respond to auditory stimuli, reward, and punishment.
source: Our starting point was the observation that auditory cortical VIP neurons respond not only to auditory stimuli but also to reward and punishment (Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pi et al., 2013.

claim: VIP interneuron activity is highly correlated with changes in pupil dilation and locomotion, suggesting a role in modulating cortical processing across arousal states.
source: Second, VIP interneuron activity is highly correlated with the changes in pupil dilation and locomotion, suggesting a role in modulating cortical processing across arousal states (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2014; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2017; Jackson et al., 2016; Pakan et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), while other reports show that locomotion modulates sensory processing independently from VIP activation (Yavorska and Wehr, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2014; Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2017; Jackson et al., 2016; Pakan et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021).

claim: Optogenetic or pharmacogenetic inhibition of VIP interneurons impairs learning and plasticity in sensory discrimination and memory-guided tasks.
source: Finally, optogenetic or pharmacogenetic inhibition (Donato et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2015; Kamigaki and Dan, 2017) of VIP interneurons, as well as their developmental dysregulation (Batista-Brito et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2015) impairs learning and plasticity in sensory discrimination and memory-guided tasks (Batista-Brito et al., 2017; Kamigaki and Dan, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Donato et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2015; Kamigaki and Dan, 2017; Batista-Brito et al., 2017).

claim: Mice learned the auditory discrimination task over 3 ± 0.6 sessions after introducing the no-go tone, reaching a performance level of 80%.
source: Mice learned this task over 3 ± 0.6 (mean ± SD) sessions after introducing the no-go tone, reaching a performance level of 80% (percentage of correct responses, Hit or CR).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the behavioral task (mean ± SD values provided).

claim: 85% of VIP interneurons responded to reward and 90% responded to punishment in the medial parietal association area.
source: We found that the majority of VIP interneurons responded to reward and punishment presentation (reward = 85%, punishment = 90%, reward and punishment = 75% of recorded VIP interneurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon imaging in the medial parietal association area.

claim: Individual VIP neurons showed a high reliability in their recruitment of 64% for Hit trials and 77% for FA trials.
source: Individual neurons showed a high reliability in their recruitment (percentage of active trials for a given neuron) of 64 and 77% for Hit and FA trials, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon imaging.

claim: 49% and 60% of VIP interneurons were simultaneously activated by reward and punishment, respectively, on individual trials.
source: Examining individual trials, 49 and 60% of VIP interneurons were simultaneously activated by reward and punishment, respectively (Figure 1D, synchronicity).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reward and punishment delivery induced an increase in activity of 29% and 10% of PV interneurons, respectively, in the medial parietal association area.
source: On the contrary, parvalbumin (PV) interneurons, another inhibitory neuron cell type, did not show comparable homogeneity in their recruitment by primary reinforcers. Reward and punishment delivery induced an increase in activity of, respectively, 29 and 10% of PV interneurons recorded in MPta (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: 83% and 85% of VIP interneurons across dorsal cortex responded to reward and punishment, respectively.
source: Among the 811 neurons imaged in 18 imaging sessions from 16 mice, 65 VIP interneurons did not show statistically significant responses to any behavioral events (e.g. auditory or visual stimulation, reward or punishment delivery) and were therefore excluded from further analyses. 83 and 85% of the remaining 746 VIP interneurons, responded to reward and punishment, respectively (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 18 imaging sessions across 16 mice, shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: 73% of VIP interneurons significantly responded to both reward and punishment.
source: We found that 73% of the VIP interneurons significantly responded to both reward and punishment, similar to our observations in MPta.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon imaging across dorsal cortex.

claim: Only 15% of VIP interneurons responded to auditory cues in Miss and CR trials.
source: Only 15% of the VIP interneurons responded to auditory cues in Miss and CR trials (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: The response of VIP interneurons to reward and punishment showed a strong correlation with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.73.
source: The response of VIP interneurons to reward and punishment showed a strong correlation (Pearson correlation coefficient for average amplitudes: 0.73, Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: On a given trial, 58% of VIP interneurons were simultaneously activated across dorsal cortex.
source: High synchronicity and reliability in VIP interneuron recruitment were also observed in our recordings extending throughout the dorsal cortex: on a given trial, 58% of VIP interneurons were simultaneously activated (57 ± 2.4% and 58 ± 2.5%, for Hit and FA trials, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VIP interneurons showed a reliability of 61% across dorsal cortex.
source: High synchronicity and reliability in VIP interneuron recruitment were also observed in our recordings extending throughout the dorsal cortex: on a given trial, 58% of VIP interneurons were simultaneously activated (57 ± 2.4% and 58 ± 2.5%, for Hit and FA trials, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) with a reliability of 61% (59 ± 1.7% and 63 ± 2.4%, for Hit and FA trials, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Calcium-related signals from VIP interneurons in the auditory cortex increased after reward and punishment delivery (Hit = 4.8 ± 0.32%, FA = 10.9 ± 0.03%).
source: Consistent with our previous electrophysiological results in ACx (Pi et al., 2013) and two-photon imaging from dorsal cortical regions, calcium-related signals from VIP interneurons in the ACx and mPFC were increased after reward and punishment delivery (in ACx: Hit = 4.8 ± 0.32%, FA = 10.9 ± 0.03%; in mPFC: Hit = 4.3 ± 0.69%, FA = 6.6 ± 0.85%, ΔF/F peaks, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Calcium-related signals from VIP interneurons in the medial prefrontal cortex increased after reward and punishment delivery (Hit = 4.3 ± 0.69%, FA = 6.6 ± 0.85%).
source: Consistent with our previous electrophysiological results in ACx (Pi et al., 2013) and two-photon imaging from dorsal cortical regions, calcium-related signals from VIP interneurons in the ACx and mPFC were increased after reward and punishment delivery (in ACx: Hit = 4.8 ± 0.32%, FA = 10.9 ± 0.03%; in mPFC: Hit = 4.3 ± 0.69%, FA = 6.6 ± 0.85%, ΔF/F peaks, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: VIP interneurons in the auditory cortex showed phasic response to reward with peak time of 0.06 ± 0.036 s and decay time constant of 2.7 s.
source: VIP interneurons in the ACx showed phasic response to reward (peak time for Hit = 0.06 ± 0.036 s, decay time constant = 2.7 s).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data analysis.

claim: Medial prefrontal VIP interneurons were slowly activated with peak time of 3.08 ± 0.968 s and decay time constant of 7.75 s.
source: In contrast, medial prefrontal VIP interneurons were slowly activated (peak time for Hit = 3.08 ± 0.968 s, decay time constant = 7.75 s, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Principal component analysis and k-means clustering delineated five functional groups of VIP interneurons based on reward response dynamics: 'fast', 'delayed', 'sustained', 'biphasic', and 'slow'.
source: We applied principal component analysis (PCA) to the average reward responses of individual neurons to reward. We then clustered these responses using k-means clustering. This approach did not readily separate neurons according to the recording sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). Rather, our clustering approach allowed us to delineate five functional groups of VIP interneurons (Figure 2F). Based on visual inspection of their mean temporal profiles, we labeled these groups as: 'fast' (n=109), 'delayed' (n=88), 'sustained' (n=177), 'biphasic' (n=120), and 'slow' (n=112).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA and k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The 'fast' group of VIP interneurons was overrepresented in parietal cortex and absent from visual cortex.
source: We observed an overrepresentation of the 'fast' group in parietal cortex and of the 'slow' group in primary visual cortex (Figure 2G). The 'fast' group was absent from visual cortex (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cluster distribution across cortical areas shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The 'slow' group of VIP interneurons was overrepresented in primary visual cortex.
source: We observed an overrepresentation of the 'fast' group in parietal cortex and of the 'slow' group in primary visual cortex (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cluster distribution across cortical areas shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The projection associated with the 'fast' group was significantly higher for VIP interneurons in parietal cortex compared to visual cortex (mean ΔPta-V1=3.22, p=3.77 10–9).
source: We found that the projection associated with the 'fast' group was significantly higher for VIP interneurons located in parietal compared to those recorded in visual cortex (mean ΔPta-V1=3.22, Mann-Whitney test, p=3.77 10–9), while the opposite was observed for the projection associated with the 'slow' group (mean ΔPta-V1=−7.79, p=3.77 10–9, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of projection data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The projection associated with the 'slow' group was significantly higher for VIP interneurons in visual cortex compared to parietal cortex (mean ΔPta-V1=−7.79, p=3.77 10–9).
source: We found that the projection associated with the 'fast' group was significantly higher for VIP interneurons located in parietal compared to those recorded in visual cortex (mean ΔPta-V1=3.22, Mann-Whitney test, p=3.77 10–9), while the opposite was observed for the projection associated with the 'slow' group (mean ΔPta-V1=−7.79, p=3.77 10–9, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of projection data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: VIP neuron soma diameter showed bimodal distributions in 7 out of 8 mice examined.
source: We addressed subtype diversity by measuring the diameter (full width at half maximum [FWHM]) of the somata and found bimodal distributions both at the level of individual mice (7/8 mice) and also the entire population examined (R2=97.7%, F=206.4, p<0.001, n=8 mice n=439 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by soma diameter measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: VIP-fast and VIP-sustained groups had somewhat larger cell bodies compared to other functional groups.
source: VIP-fast and VIP-sustained groups had somewhat larger cell bodies (fast: 10.2 ± 0.4 µm, delayed: 9.8 ± 0.2 µm, sustained: 10.4 ± 0.2 µm, biphasic: 10.0 ± 0.2 µm, slow: 9.4 ± 0.2 µm, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), further supporting the possibility that some of the identified functional VIP groups correspond to distinct genetic VIP interneuron subtypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by soma diameter measurements across functional groups shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Tensor component analysis identified a latent temporal component that robustly separated Hit and FA trials from Miss and CR trials (meanMiss&CR vs meanHit&FA=0.02 vs 0.2, p<0.001).
source: We found a latent temporal component that robustly separated Hit and FA trials from Miss and CR trials (second component, Figure 2H, meanMiss&CR vs meanHit&FA=0.02 vs 0.2, Mann-Whitney test, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by tensor component analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The third latent temporal component from tensor component analysis showed a slower time course with some reward specificity and was overrepresented in neurons from visual cortex (meanSS,Mtr,Pta vs meanV1=0.02 vs 0.06 p<0.001).
source: The third latent temporal component showed a slower time course, with some reward specificity and was overrepresented in neurons from the visual cortex (meanSS,Mtr,Pta vs meanV1=0.02 vs 0.06 p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by tensor component analysis.

claim: There was a positive correlation between hit rate and the magnitude of cue response of VIP interneurons during Hit trials (R=0.62).
source: We observed a positive correlation between the hit rate and the magnitude of the cue response of VIP interneurons during Hit trials (R=0.62, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Hit rate explained 39% of the variance of cue responses in VIP interneurons (R2=39.0%; p=0.006).
source: Using a simple linear regression model, we found that the hit rate was able to explain 39% of the variance of cue responses (R2=39.0%; p=0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis.

claim: Reinforcement delivery associated with larger changes in pupil diameter led to stronger recruitment of VIP interneurons in somatosensory cortex (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 40 vs 29%, p=0.01).
source: Reinforcement delivery associated with larger changes in pupil diameter led to a stronger recruitment of VIP interneurons in both the SS (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 40 vs 29% n=26, t-test, p=0.01) and Mtr cortex (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 28 vs 18%, n=111, p<0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupil dilation groups shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reinforcement delivery associated with larger changes in pupil diameter led to stronger recruitment of VIP interneurons in motor cortex (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 28 vs 18%, p<0.001).
source: Reinforcement delivery associated with larger changes in pupil diameter led to a stronger recruitment of VIP interneurons in both the SS (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 40 vs 29% n=26, t-test, p=0.01) and Mtr cortex (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 28 vs 18%, n=111, p<0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupil dilation groups shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reinforcer-mediated responses in medial prefrontal cortex were significantly larger in trials with greater changes in pupil diameter (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 3.8 vs 1.4%, p=0.01).
source: Indeed, reinforcer-mediated responses in mPFC were significantly larger in trials with greater changes in pupil diameter (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 3.8 vs 1.4%, n=6 mice, p=0.01; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pupil size-dependent modulation of reward responses was absent in auditory cortex recordings (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 4.5 vs 3.2%, p=0.08).
source: This pupil size-dependent modulation was, however, absent in recordings of VIP interneurons in the ACx (large vs small pupil ΔF/F: 4.5 vs 3.2%, n=6 mice, p=0.08 in the ACx; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VIP interneuron responses to reward were stronger when mice ran faster in somatosensory cortex (high vs low speed change ΔF/F: 42 vs 27%, p<0.001).
source: Similar to what we observed with the pupil size, VIP interneuron responses to reward were stronger when the mice ran faster both for SS (high vs low speed change ΔF/F: 42 vs 27% n=26, t-test, p<0.001) and Mtr cortex-located interneurons (high vs low speed change ΔF/F 30 vs 19%, n=86, p<0.001, Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing running speed groups shown in Figure 3G.

claim: VIP interneuron responses to reward were stronger when mice ran faster in motor cortex (high vs low speed change ΔF/F: 30 vs 19%, p<0.001).
source: Similar to what we observed with the pupil size, VIP interneuron responses to reward were stronger when the mice ran faster both for SS (high vs low speed change ΔF/F: 42 vs 27% n=26, t-test, p<0.001) and Mtr cortex-located interneurons (high vs low speed change ΔF/F 30 vs 19%, n=86, p<0.001, Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing running speed groups shown in Figure 3G.

claim: VIP interneuron population activity was modulated by running speed in medial prefrontal cortex (high vs low speed change, ΔF/F: 5 vs 3.5%, p=0.02).
source: VIP interneuron population activity was modulated by running speed in mPFC (high vs low speed change, ΔF/F: 5 vs 3.5%, p=0.02) but not in ACx (ΔF/F: 5.4 vs 4.1%, p=0.44) similar to what found for pupil modulation (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VIP interneuron population activity was not modulated by running speed in auditory cortex (ΔF/F: 5.4 vs 4.1%, p=0.44).
source: VIP interneuron population activity was modulated by running speed in mPFC (high vs low speed change, ΔF/F: 5 vs 3.5%, p=0.02) but not in ACx (ΔF/F: 5.4 vs 4.1%, p=0.44) similar to what found for pupil modulation (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A generalized linear model explained 18.8 ± 11.1% of the variance of VIP population calcium signal.
source: This model was able to explain 18.8 ± 11.1% of the variance of the VIP population calcium signal and highlighted that arousal was the best predictor, followed by reward, punishment, locomotion velocity, and auditory cue (weights = 0.055, 0.031, 0.028, 0.020, and 0.018, respectively; all predictors, except the auditory cue in the case of one animal contributed significantly, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by generalized linear model analysis.

claim: In the generalized linear model, arousal was the best predictor of VIP activity (weight = 0.055), followed by reward (0.031), punishment (0.028), locomotion velocity (0.020), and auditory cue (0.018).
source: This model was able to explain 18.8 ± 11.1% of the variance of the VIP population calcium signal and highlighted that arousal was the best predictor, followed by reward, punishment, locomotion velocity, and auditory cue (weights = 0.055, 0.031, 0.028, 0.020, and 0.018, respectively; all predictors, except the auditory cue in the case of one animal contributed significantly, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by generalized linear model analysis.

claim: 93.5% of VIP interneurons in visual cortex responded to visual stimuli.
source: The vast majority of VIP interneurons (93.5%) responded to visual stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from visual stimulation experiments.

claim: VIP interneurons showed broad tuning with little or no preferred directions or orientation (OSI = 0.17 ± 0.01, DSI = 0.16 ± 0.01).
source: As previously reported (Kerlin et al., 2010; Mesik et al., 2015), VIP interneurons showed broad tuning with little or no preferred directions or orientation (OSI = 0.17 ± 0.01, DSI = 0.16 ± 0.01, Figure 4C) especially compared to pyramidal cells (OSI = 0.63 ± 0.01, t-test, p<0.001, DSI = 0.34 ± 0.01, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from visual stimulation experiments shown in Figure 4C, and is consistent with prior reports (Kerlin et al., 2010; Mesik et al., 2015).

claim: Pyramidal cells showed higher orientation and direction selectivity (OSI = 0.63 ± 0.01, DSI = 0.34 ± 0.01) compared to VIP interneurons.
source: As previously reported (Kerlin et al., 2010; Mesik et al., 2015), VIP interneurons showed broad tuning with little or no preferred directions or orientation (OSI = 0.17 ± 0.01, DSI = 0.16 ± 0.01, Figure 4C) especially compared to pyramidal cells (OSI = 0.63 ± 0.01, t-test, p<0.001, DSI = 0.34 ± 0.01, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from visual stimulation experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 80.4% of VIP neurons in visual cortex were significantly activated by reward or punishment.
source: We found that 80.4% of VIP neurons were significantly activated by reward or punishment with a response magnitude comparable to their visual responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from visual cortex recordings during the auditory discrimination task.

claim: Reinforcement-evoked responses were only weakly correlated with visual stimulus-evoked responses (Pearson's R value for reward and punishment combined: 0.22, R2=0.05, F=8.3, p=0.005).
source: The reinforcement-evoked responses were only weakly correlated with visual stimulus-evoked responses (Pearson's R value for reward: 0.16, for punishment: 0.23, and reward and punishment combined: 0.22, R2=0.05, F=8.3, p=0.005; Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither orientation nor direction selectivity of VIP neurons correlated with their reinforcement responses (Pearson's R value for OSI: 0.08, p=0.31, for DSI: 0.06, p=0.45).
source: Neither the orientation nor the direction selectivity of the VIP neurons correlated with their reinforcement responses (Pearson's R value for OSI: 0.08, p=0.31, for DSI: 0.06, p=0.45; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Chessboard scanning provides a ~170-fold increase in measurement speed and ~15-fold increase in SNR compared to a high-speed resonant mirror-based system scanning the same volume.
source: Overall, chessboard scanning produces an additional ~170-fold increase in measurement speed and ~15-fold increase in SNR, compared to a high-speed resonant mirror-based system scanning the same volume (Table S1).
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical calculations comparing scanning methods shown in Table S1.

claim: 3D chessboard scanning can result in over 5000-fold increase in SNR² or measurement speed when compared to point-by-point volume scanning.
source: This means that we can get over 5000-fold increase in SNR2 or in the measurement speed (or even in the product of both) when AO-based 3D ROI scanning is used instead of point-by-point volume scanning.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical calculations in the Methods section.

claim: The 3D chessboard scanning method could image 120 neurons at 27.7 Hz.
source: The 3D chessboard scanning method could image the 120 chessboards at 27.7 Hz (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1, Table S1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Table S1.

claim: Point-by-point volume scanning of the same 120 neurons would have a measurement speed of only 0.00062 Hz, representing a 44,762-fold lower measurement speed compared to chessboard scanning.
source: However, the measurement speed was only 0.00062 Hz when the same 120 neurons were recorded using point-by-point volume scanning when using the same, relatively long, pixel dwell time (30 µs). This means a 44,762-fold lower measurement speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by theoretical calculations comparing scanning methods.

claim: VIP cells have been reported to respond to reward in hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex and to foot shock in amygdala.
source: VIP cells have been reported to respond to reward in hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and to foot shock in amygdala (Krabbe et al., 2019; Pinto and Dan, 2015; Turi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Krabbe et al., 2019; Pinto and Dan, 2015; Turi et al., 2019).

claim: Reinforcer-induced activation of VIP interneurons is likely to produce a net disinhibitory effect.
source: Nevertheless, reinforcer-induced activation of VIP interneurons, is likely to produce a net disinhibitory effect (Lee et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013) and thereby provide gain modulation (Pi et al., 2013) through changing the balance of inhibition across the somato-dendritic axis (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lee et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013) and inference from known circuit mechanisms.

claim: VIP-mediated disinhibition through somatostatin interneurons will preferentially boost dendritic spikes.
source: Indeed, VIP-mediated disinhibition through somatostatin interneurons will preferentially boost dendritic spikes (Larkum et al., 2009; Lavzin et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Larkum et al., 2009; Lavzin et al., 2012; Palmer et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2013).

claim: Central cholinergic neurons convey rapid reinforcement responses to cortex.
source: Indeed, central cholinergic neurons convey rapid reinforcement responses to cortex (Hangya et al., 2015), and a type of layer 1 inhibitory neuron is activated by punishment through a nicotinic mechanism (Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Hangya et al., 2015; Letzkus et al., 2011).

claim: VIP neurons express fast, ionotropic nicotinic receptors and can be activated by acetylcholine in vitro.
source: VIP neurons express fast, ionotropic nicotinic receptors and can be activated by acetylcholine in vitro (Alitto and Dan, 2012; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Alitto and Dan, 2012; Chen et al., 2015).

claim: Optogenetic cholinergic stimulation can depolarize the membrane potential of VIP neurons in vivo.
source: Optogenetic cholinergic stimulation can also depolarize the membrane potential of VIP neurons in vivo (Gasselin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Gasselin et al., 2021).

claim: Cholinergic activity in the neocortex was necessary for learning and modulated VIP cells during locomotor activity.
source: Cholinergic activity in the neocortex was necessary for learning and modulated VIP cells during locomotor activity (Ren et al., 2022), and potentially also responsible for the co-activation in the auditory discrimination task.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Ren et al., 2022).

claim: Many VIP neurons express 5HT3A, the ionotropic serotonin receptor.
source: Indeed, many (but not all) VIP neurons express 5HT3A, the ionotropic serotonin receptor, which could rapidly transduce information via serotonergic neuromodulation (Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Tasic et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018).

claim: The global activation of VIP interneurons early in learning may form a new information channel for cortical learning and explain how organism-level information about reinforcers regulates local circuit processing and plasticity.
source: By signaling reinforcement events, the global activation of VIP interneurons early in learning, may form a new information channel for cortical learning and explain how organism-level information about reinforcers regulates local circuit processing and plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: VIP-mediated feedback signaling could provide the required global learning signal to strengthen functional connectivity across cortical representations.
source: In other words, the VIP-mediated feedback signaling could provide the required global learning signal to strengthen functional connectivity across cortical representations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: VIP neurons may transiently dial up the gain on learning, similar to how different learning phases are controlled in deep neural networks in artificial intelligence.
source: In this way, VIP neurons may transiently dial up the gain on learning, similar to how different learning phases are controlled in deep neural networks in artificial intelligence (Guerguiev et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and analogy to artificial intelligence, supported by a citation (Guerguiev et al., 2017).
